planting.note: Plant dormant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall into shallow, rocky or gravelly soil on an open, south-facing slope; established clumps can also be divided just after bloom while still in leaf.

directions: Grass widow is among the very first wildflowers to open on the thin, rocky prairies and mossy balds of the San Juan Islands and Puget Sound shoreline, its satiny violet-pink blooms appearing on bare ground before the surrounding grass greens up. Each flower lasts only a few days but a clump produces a long succession of buds through late winter into early spring. The grasslike foliage and corm die back completely by early summer, so the planting site must be allowed to dry out and bake through the dormant season rather than receiving any supplemental irrigation. Give it the thinnest, most mineral soil available and full sun exposure, mimicking the shallow glacial till and exposed bedrock where it grows wild.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly into its permanent position in fall so it experiences a full winter of cold, damp chilling before germinating the following spring; the thick taproot resents any later transplanting.

directions: This large, deep-rooted member of the carrot family is a conspicuous early-spring presence on rocky Garry oak balds and talus slopes around the Salish Sea, sending up finely divided, almost fern-like foliage topped by dense clusters of maroon to chocolate-brown flowers that stand out among the more typical yellow-flowered lomatiums. The stout taproot can persist for decades once established, storing the reserves the plant needs to flower through dry Pacific Northwest summers with no irrigation at all. Because the taproot is easily damaged, seed should always be sown where the plant is meant to stay rather than started in containers for later transplant. Expect a slow start: plants commonly take several years to reach flowering size from seed, so patience is part of growing this species well.

subcategory: Pacific Northwest native rock-garden prairie wildflower

planting.note: Sow seed on the surface of lean, mineral soil in fall and leave uncovered through winter, or set out nursery divisions in early spring into a shallow-soil rock garden or gravel bed.

directions: A small, ground-hugging rosette-former typical of the thin, mossy soil pockets on rocky Garry oak prairie outcrops, this saxifrage sends up short, wiry stems topped with tight clusters of small white flowers in early spring. The fleshy basal leaves stay low and tight against the rock, helping the plant survive baking summer sun on sites with almost no soil depth. It goes fully dormant by midsummer and should never be watered during that rest period, since standing moisture around the crown in warm weather quickly causes rot. Rock garden and crevice garden growers value it for exactly the kind of shallow, gritty, fast-draining pocket that stumps most other perennials.

planting.note: Root dormant hardwood cuttings over winter or set out a rooted transplant in spring against a trellis, fence, or shrub it can scramble over; thin, rocky caliche soil is tolerated as long as drainage is sharp.

directions: Panhandle grape is the wild grapevine of the juniper-and-mesquite breaks along the rims of Palo Duro and the Caprock Canyonlands, scrambling over rock outcrops and shrubs with maple-shaped, pale-undersided leaves that give the species its name. It tolerates thin, rocky, lime-rich canyon soils that would stunt most cultivated grapes and needs no irrigation once its roots reach the rimrock crevices it favors in the wild. Small, tart purple-black grapes ripen in late summer and are prized for jelly and wine as well as for the wildlife they feed; a sturdy support is essential since the vine climbs vigorously rather than forming a self-supporting shrub. Prune hard in late winter to control its spread and encourage the vigorous new growth that carries the most fruit.

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed or set out a nursery transplant in spring into sharply drained, rocky or caliche soil; established clumps can also be divided from spreading rhizomes.

directions: Vine ephedra forms sprawling, wiry, jointed green stems that scramble over rock and through sparse grass on the gypsum and caliche breaks below canyon rims in the Texas Panhandle, staying leafless year-round and photosynthesizing through its stems like its better-known Mormon tea relatives. Small conelike structures appear at the stem joints in spring, followed on female plants by fleshy, reddish, berry-like seed cones that distinguish it from drier, more papery-coned ephedras. It spreads slowly outward by rhizome as well as by seed, eventually forming a loose, tangled colony that needs no supplemental water once rooted into native canyon-rim soil. Give it full sun and lean, gravelly or caliche soil, and leave it room to sprawl rather than confining it to a tight bed.
